fields.h1: Build Agency Workflow Automation for Every Client Account
fields.hero_description: Build agency workflow automation that tracks revision rounds, ad spend, and retainer hours for every client account.
fields.features_heading: What Emergent Builds Into an Agency App
fields.features_subheading: Agency workflow automation runs the counting and chasing behind each client account, and leaves the creative calls to your team.
fields.feature_1:
Write each client's rules in a prompt

Describe the rules the way you would brief a new account manager, such as how many revision rounds a contract includes. Emergent builds the app, its database, and its logic.
fields.feature_2:
A count of revision rounds on every proof

Each round of client changes is logged against the job. When a request goes past the rounds in the contract, the app marks it out of scope and tells the account lead.
fields.feature_3:
Connects to ad accounts and time trackers

The app connects to any tool with an API, so spend comes in from the ad accounts and hours from the time tracker. Data syncs in and out, and nobody copies numbers by hand.
fields.feature_4:
Alerts that name the person who acts

Pick who hears about each rule and where: a media buyer in Slack, an account lead by email, a freelancer in the app. Unanswered alerts turn into reminders, then escalations.
fields.feature_5:
One live board across client accounts

The dashboard shows every client's spend, retainer hours, and open revision requests, updated live. The records sit in a database you own, and last year's accounts stay on hand.
fields.feature_6:
The agency app's code, in your GitHub

Export the full code of the app to your GitHub repository on paid plans. A developer on your team can read every pacing rule and hours rule before the account leads rely on them.
fields.why_description: Emergent builds the revision log and the client board as one app, with no task cap on how often the rules run.

fields.tab_content_1:
The third proof round goes to the account lead

Ostrander Cycles returns the spring campaign proof on April 3 with a third round of changes. Its contract includes 2 revision rounds. The app logs round 3 as out of scope, and Juno Achterberg, the account lead, gets a Slack direct message with a Draft change request button before anyone edits.
fields.tab_content_2:
Ad spend for Pembrook passes half by March 14

Pembrook Dental budgets $12,000 for March ads across search and social. By March 14 the connected ad accounts show $7,800 spent. Any client over half its budget before the 15th sets off an alert, and Idris Kowalczyk, the media buyer, gets it in Slack with the spend by campaign.
fields.tab_content_3:
34 of 40 retainer hours gone by October 20

Marrowgate Coffee pays for 40 hours of design and copy work a month. By October 20 the team has logged 34 of them in the time tracker. The alert fires at 30 hours, and Wilhelmina Szabo, the account lead, gets an email with the hours by person before she plans the last 11 days.
fields.tab_content_4:
Motion job goes to Cassius in 38 minutes

A 6-hour motion graphics job for Ostrander Cycles arrives at 11:02 a.m. while both in-house designers are booked. The app offers it to the 3 freelancers tagged Motion, with 2 hours to accept. Cassius Eberhardt accepts at 11:40 a.m., and the brief and the due date go to him in the app.

fields.howto_title: How to Build Agency Workflow Automation
fields.howto_description: Seven steps that take agency workflow automation from one client account to four rules your account leads run every month.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Pick one account from last month
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Set a pacing rule for ad budgets
fields.howto_step_1_des: Choose an account that kept your team busy and list every step someone did by hand: counting revision rounds, checking ad spend, adding up hours, and finding cover when designers were full. Start with the steps that follow a fixed rule.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Open each client contract and note how many revision rounds it includes and what counts as one round. Decide who hears about a request past that limit, and whether the work waits for a signed change request.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Pick the point where spend is too far ahead of the calendar, such as more than half the budget before the 15th. Choose who gets the alert for each client, and whether it goes to Slack or email.
fields.howto_step_4_des: For each retainer, pick the hour count that triggers an alert to the account lead, leaving enough hours to finish the month's planned work. Decide whether a second alert goes out when the retainer is fully used.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Tag your freelancer pool by skill
fields.howto_step_5_des: List the freelancers you call when the in-house team is full, and tag each with skills such as motion, copy, or illustration. Pick how long an offer stays open and what happens when nobody accepts in time.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Describe the workflow in one prompt
fields.howto_step_6_des: Write the rules from the last four steps as plain sentences, with the real numbers from each contract and budget. Emergent builds the app from that prompt, alerts and client board included, and you change any rule later by prompting again.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Run last month's proofs and logged hours through the app before anyone depends on it. Check that each alert would have reached the right person on the right day. Fix any rule that fired too early or too late, then run the month again.

faq_plan.a: Agency workflow automation is the use of software to automatically execute defined sequences of tasks within an agency. A trigger, such as a client returning a proof, starts the next step, like a message to the media buyer or a task for a named person. People keep the creative direction and the client conversations.

faq_plan.q: How do I set up agency workflow automation?
faq_plan.a: Start with one client account and list the steps that run the same way every time, such as counting revision rounds. Describe those rules in a prompt to Emergent's AI automation builder, and Emergent builds the app with its database and client board. Test it on a month of real requests first.

faq_plan.q: What are some agency workflow automation examples?
faq_plan.a: Four examples: logging revision rounds against the contract, alerting a media buyer when ad spend runs ahead, warning an account lead before retainer hours run out, and offering overflow jobs to freelancers. Agencies run on repeatable processes: client onboarding, project kickoffs, status updates, approvals, invoicing. Each of those can get its own rule.

faq_plan.q: Which tasks should agency workflow automation handle first?
faq_plan.a: Automate the tasks that follow a fixed rule and repeat every week, like counting revision rounds or checking spend against a budget. Keep creative direction and pricing talks with people. The same test of a fixed, repeated rule picks the first flow for a school in education workflow automation.

faq_plan.q: How does agency workflow automation track revision rounds?
faq_plan.a: Store each contract's included rounds on the client record and log every set of changes as a numbered round on the job. A request beyond the limit is flagged for the account lead, who decides whether to send a change request; the rule never refuses the client on its own.

faq_plan.q: Can agency workflow automation track ad spend pacing?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Connect the ad platforms you use, where they offer an API, and set a monthly budget per client. The app compares each client's spend with the calendar every day and alerts the media buyer when spend runs ahead of your rule. Emergent puts no task cap on these checks: 40 clients get the same daily check as 4.

faq_plan.q: How does agency workflow automation warn before retainer hours run out?
faq_plan.a: Pull logged hours from your time tracker and set an alert point below each retainer's total. Then decide what the lead does next: move work to next month, or send the client an hours estimate to approve. The same kind of timed alert moves an uncalled buyer lead in real estate workflow automation.

faq_plan.q: Can agency workflow automation route overflow work to freelancers?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Tag each freelancer by skill, then have the app offer a new job to everyone with the matching tag and give it to the first one to accept within your window. If nobody accepts in time, the app escalates to the studio lead. Every offer and answer is saved in a database you own, which shows over time who says yes.

faq_plan.q: What client data does agency workflow automation need?
faq_plan.a: Store only what the rules need: contract terms such as included rounds and retainer hours, monthly ad budgets, logged hours by person, and the freelancer pool with skills. Leave client ad account logins in the ad platforms themselves. Emergent has SOC 2 Type I and ISO 27001.

faq_plan.q: Can a small agency use workflow automation without a developer?
faq_plan.a: Yes. You describe the rules in plain sentences, and Emergent turns that prompt into a working app. A three-person agency can start with one rule, such as the revision count, and add pacing and hours later. The same one-rule start works for a small law office in legal workflow automation.

plan.angle: The top 10 split between people selling automation services (an AI automation agency, a services firm), a glossary definition and tool roundups that list apps without showing one workflow running. This page follows one marketing agency, Tallowfield Creative, through four flows only an agency runs: a third revision round on a client proof that the app logs as out of scope, ad spend pacing ahead of the month on a client account, a retainer that reaches 80% of its hours by the 20th, and an overflow motion job offered to the freelancer pool. The FAQ answers the setup, scope, pacing, retainer, freelancer, data and testing questions an agency operations lead asks, and leaves onboarding, content production and project handoffs to their own pages.
